Dambulla: Ancient caves carved
into the rock

I almost didn’t go to Dambulla.

It wasn’t part of some carefully planned itinerary. I was staying in Rekawa, enjoying the slower rhythm of the south, when Pubudu convinced me that we should go.

So one day, I got on the back of his scooter and we set off.

The journey itself became part
of the memory.

And then, after the long ride from Rekawa, we reached Dambulla.

I had no idea how much I was about
to love it.

More than a temple

Dambulla is not the kind of place you fully understand from the outside.

The caves are hidden within a huge rock, and reaching them is part of the experience. You climb up through the trees, leave the busy road behind and slowly make your way towards one of Sri Lanka’s most important Buddhist sites.

The Rangiri Dambulla Cave Temple has been a place of Buddhist worship and pilgrimage for more than two thousand years. Today, the complex includes five main cave shrines, filled with Buddha statues and ancient murals. UNESCO describes it as the largest and best-preserved cave-temple complex in Sri Lanka.

But even knowing that, I don’t think anything really prepares you
for what you see inside.

Because this is not simply a collection of rooms with statues.

You are standing inside the rock.

The climb is part of the story

Before we could enter the sacred caves, there was one important thing left to do.

Climb.

And let me tell you something: getting to the top is one thing. Getting back down is another story.

The path leads you up through the greenery and stone steps, and at the time I remember thinking mostly about one thing: How am I going to get back
down from here?

My knees were already negotiating with the rest of my body.

At one point, I honestly considered rolling down the hill. It seemed faster and, in that particular moment, possibly less painful.

But the climb creates something important. By the time you reach the caves, you have left the road, the noise and everyday life below you. There is a feeling of arriving somewhere separate from the rest
of the world.

And then you enter.

Inside the rock

This was the moment when Dambulla completely won me over.

The caves are dark and cool. The ceiling curves naturally above you, covered with paintings. Buddha statues fill the space. Some are sitting. Some are standing. And one of the most striking images is the large reclining Buddha, stretching across the cave in glowing shades of gold.

Everywhere you look, there is something to take in.

Ancient paintings cover large sections of the walls and ceilings, while the statues create a space that feels both artistic and deeply spiritual. Across the five caves, the murals cover around 2,100 square metres, and the complex contains 157 statues.

But numbers don’t really explain Dambulla.

The feeling does.

You walk slowly because there is too much to see at once. The rock above you, the paintings, the statues, the soft
light, the silence.

For a moment, it is easy to forget that you are inside a temple that has been welcoming pilgrims for centuries.

A living place of faith

This was something I understood even more clearly because of Pubudu.

Before we entered the sacred area, he bought me flowers.

We carried them up with us and left them as an offering near the Buddha.

It was a small moment, but it changed the way I saw the place.

Dambulla was not simply something I had come to see.

It was not just another historical site where tourists arrive, take photographs
and move on.

People still come here to pray.

They still bring offerings.

The caves are still used for Buddhist rituals, continuing a tradition that has lasted for more than two millennia.

And suddenly, standing there with flowers in my hands, I understood that I wasn’t
just visiting history.

I was standing inside something that was still alive.

What to know before you go

If you are visiting Dambulla, remember that this is a sacred place.

You should dress respectfully, with your knees and shoulders covered. I had to cover my legs, and I was given a large shawl to wear before entering.

You will also need to remove your shoes before entering the sacred areas.

That meant walking barefoot.

And yes, after climbing all those steps, my feet probably had a few opinions
about that too.

But honestly, it is part of the experience.

That barefoot moment stayed with me longer than I expected. After Dambulla, I found myself walking barefoot whenever I could. There was something about it that simply felt right, a small kind of freedom I had never really noticed before.

The best thing you can do is come prepared: wear something comfortable for the climb and bring a light scarf or shawl with you in case you need to cover up.

And once you are inside, slow down.

This is not a place to rush through.

Sri Lanka’s general guidance for visiting religious sites recommends covering shoulders and clothing below the knees, as well as removing footwear before entering temples and sacred areas.

A hidden gem worth the climb

Dambulla is famous, of course. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most important cultural places in Sri Lanka.

And yet, for me, it still felt like discovering something hidden.

Maybe it was because the caves are literally concealed inside the rock.

Maybe it was because I hadn’t
planned the visit.

Or maybe it was because the best places are sometimes the ones you almost miss.

I had travelled all the way from Rekawa on the back of a scooter with someone I had only recently met, trusting him enough to let him take me somewhere I knew almost nothing about.

That journey became one of my favourite memories from Sri Lanka.

Not because everything was easy.

The climb was not easy.

The way back down was definitely not easy.

My legs were questioning every decision I had ever made.

But then there were the caves.

The paintings.

The reclining Buddha.

The flowers we carried to the top.

And the feeling of standing inside a place that had been sacred to generations of people long before I arrived.

Why part of me
stayed in Dambulla

There are places you visit and remember because they were beautiful.

And then there are places that stay with you for reasons you can’t completely explain.

Dambulla is one of those places for me.

Maybe it was the adventure of getting there.

Maybe it was Pubudu convincing me to go.

Maybe it was the long scooter ride from Rekawa, through a part of Sri Lanka I would probably never have seen otherwise.

Maybe it was the kindness that made me trust a person I had only just met enough to climb onto the back of his scooter and disappear down the road with him.

Or maybe it was simply the moment when I stepped inside those caves
and looked up.

Whatever the reason, I left with the feeling that I had found something special.

And somewhere between the climb, the bare feet, the enormous shawl around my legs and my dramatic plans to roll back down the hill, a small part of my

soul stayed there.

A few moments from my visit

Some places are difficult to explain. Sometimes, the best way to remember them is simply through the moments you brought home.
